title: PostgreSQL pgvector and EF Core
why: Lecture 9's vectors are in memory: they disappear on restart, and the search compares every dish one by one. In a real system vectors are stored in the database and the search runs with an index. Today we teach PostgreSQL to “understand” vectors with pgvector, store and search them with EF Core, and create an HNSW index. This is the storage for RAG (lecture 11).
outcomes: You'll explain what a vector database is and why we use PostgreSQL with pgvector instead of a separate vector database
You'll add a `vector(768)` column with EF Core (`Pgvector.EntityFrameworkCore`, `UseVector`, a migration) and write vectors to the database
You'll write a semantic search in LINQ (`CosineDistance`) and explain why distance = 1 − similarity
You'll create an HNSW index, check it with `EXPLAIN` and explain what approximate search and recall mean

review.q: What three problems do vectors kept in memory have?
review.a: They disappear on restart — everything is calculated again · the search compares everything one by one (O(n)) · the data is in two places — the description changes, the vector stays old

review.q: What does `<=>` measure, and why do we sort ascending?
review.a: cosine distance = 1 − similarity · 0 — the same direction · a small distance = close, so ORDER BY distance ASC · score 0.71 → distance 0.29
One model — one map · when the model changes we know which vectors need recalculating · indexing calculates only those (and the nulls)

review.q: What does it mean that HNSW is approximate? What is recall?
review.a: ANN — it doesn't compare everything, it searches a graph by “floors”; very fast, but it can occasionally miss a correct one · recall — what share of the exact search results it found

review.q: You created an HNSW index, but `EXPLAIN` shows a `Seq Scan`. Two possible reasons?
review.a: The operator doesn't match the search (vector_l2_ops vs CosineDistance) · the table is small — a seq scan is cheaper for the planner, that's normal

quiz.q: Lecture 9's search vectors are in the `MenuController`'s `static` list. What happens after a deploy?
options: The vectors disappear and the whole menu has to be sent to the embedding model again
The vectors move to the database
quiz.explain: Memory belongs to the app's process — on restart everything is calculated again.

quiz.q: Why do we use pgvector instead of a separate vector database (Qdrant)?
options: We already have PostgreSQL: the vector next to the dish, in the same table — one transaction, one backup, WHERE and JOIN
quiz.explain: A separate vector database makes sense at large scale or when the data isn't in PostgreSQL.

quiz.q: In lecture 9 the score was 0.71. What will pgvector's `<=>` return?
quiz.explain: A small distance = close, so ORDER BY is ascending.

quiz.q: What do we need `UseVector()` in `UseNpgsql` for?
options: So that Npgsql knows pgvector's `vector` type and maps it to C#'s `Vector`
quiz.explain: HasPostgresExtension("vector") creates the CREATE EXTENSION in the migration.

quiz.q: You called `/menu/embeddings` a second time and got `count: 0`. Why?
options: Indexing only calculates what has no vector or has one from another model — everything already has one
quiz.explain: The vectors are in the database — no more money is spent.

options: In C#, after loading every dish
In the database: in SQL, ORDER BY "Embedding" <=> @query LIMIT 3 — only 3 rows come to C#

quiz.q: The index uses `vector_l2_ops`, the search uses `CosineDistance`. What happens?
options: The search works, but the index isn't used — it will be slow
quiz.explain: The index operator must match the search function: vector_cosine_ops ↔ CosineDistance.

quiz.q: The dish and the price are in PostgreSQL, and we want a filter “up to 20 lari”. Which way is better?
options: EF Core + pgvector: WHERE Price <= 20 and ORDER BY distance — one query
Two databases and merging the results in C#
